correctness.rationale: Writing A_r=P_{2^r+1}, the recurrence gives A_r=X+A_{r-1}(X²), with A_1=1+X, so A_r has exactly the displayed support. For B_r=P_{2^r+3}, its odd-index terms are X(A_r−X) and A_r−X−X² by one further even-index substitution. Thus B_r mod A_r is −X(1+2X). Since A_r(t)≡1 mod t, the factor t can be discarded from the integer gcd (at t=0 the value A_r(0)=1). For the nonzero odd modulus |2t+1|, multiplying by 2^d permits evaluation at −1/2 with no change in gcd; the resulting integer is R_r. Its distinct binary exponents include zero, so t↦2t+1 bijects residue classes mod R_r. Totient counting gives the spectrum, and the unique class attaining R_r forces every period to be divisible by R_r. For the signed resultant, take the product of −α(1+2α) over the roots of the monic A_r. The −α factors have product A_r(0)=1, and the remaining product is (−1)^d 2^d A_r(−1/2)=R_r since d is even, including r=2. Monicity protects the degrees in every reduction; the common-root criterion applies, including p=2, which never divides R_r.

value.rationale: This is the first gap beyond consecutive indices, anchored at the canonical dyadic sparse polynomial. There is a nontrivial obstruction to arithmetic coprimality even though the pair is coprime over characteristic zero. A single explicit sparse binary integer determines exactly which primes can cause collisions and when every possible value gcd occurs. This supplies usable arithmetic information for a natural family at arbitrary index, not just a finite table or a recomputation of the general resultant criterion.
residual_risks: No general factorization of R_r or statement for arbitrary index pairs follows from the reviewed claim.
